subsection: 8. Industrialisation, economic crisis and revolution in Tsarist Russia, 1871–1920

notes.h: Tsarist Russia in 1871: autocracy and backwardness
notes.b: Russia was the largest state in Europe, but it was poor, overwhelmingly rural and ruled by an autocratic tsar. To see why it later faced crisis and revolution, you need to know how it was governed and how far behind the West it had fallen.
points: Autocracy means the tsar ruled with no parliament and no constitution before 1905. He was backed by the Orthodox Church, the nobility, the army, the bureaucracy and the secret police (the Okhrana), so there was no legal way to challenge him.
Defeat in the Crimean War (1853-56) convinced the government that Russia must modernise, because its army and economy could not match Britain and France. This led to the reforms of Alexander II.

The emancipation of the serfs (peasants bound to their landlords) in 1861 was Alexander II's greatest reform. Peasants had to make redemption payments to the state over 49 years for the land they received, which left many in debt.

Most peasants held land in the mir (the village commune), which periodically redistributed strips among households. This discouraged investment, because no one kept the same land long enough to improve it, so farming methods stayed backward.
The census of 1897 showed about 126 million people, about four-fifths of them peasants. Russia was a multinational empire, and ethnic Russians were under half the population.
In 1871 Russia had little heavy industry, few railways for its size and a weak banking system. It exported grain and relied on foreign capital (money invested from abroad) and technology.

Alexander II's other reforms, such as the zemstva (elected local councils, from 1864), the courts and the army, were limited. He was assassinated in St Petersburg on 13 March 1881 (1 March in the Russian calendar) by the revolutionary group People's Will (Narodnaya Volya).

Alexander III (1881-94) and Nicholas II (1894-1917) upheld autocracy and pursued Russification, forcing the Russian language and officials on minorities such as Poles and Finns. In January 1895 Nicholas told zemstvo delegates that hopes of a share in government were 'senseless dreams'.
notes.tip: Ordinary-level paragraphs on peasant conditions are expected to give dates: emancipation in 1861, redemption payments over 49 years and the mir. Use these dated facts rather than general statements about poverty.

notes.h: Two calendars and two names for the capital
notes.b: Russian dates and names can confuse you, because Russia ran on a different calendar and its capital changed names. Getting these right explains why the 'February' and 'October' revolutions happened in March and November.
points: Russia used the old (Julian) calendar, which was 12 days behind the Western (Gregorian) calendar in the nineteenth century and 13 days behind in the twentieth. The Bolsheviks adopted the Western calendar in February 1918, when 31 January was followed by 14 February.
Western dates come first with the Russian date in brackets. This is why the February Revolution took place in March 1917 and the October Revolution in November 1917.
St Petersburg was renamed Petrograd in 1914, so use the name that is correct for the date. The capital moved from Petrograd to Moscow in March 1918.
notes.tip: Always say which calendar a date uses. A date such as 17 October 1905 is the Russian date, and the Western date is 30 October.

notes.h: Opposition to the tsar: parties working underground
notes.b: With no parliament and no legal opposition, those who wanted change had to organise in secret. By 1905 three main groups had formed, and they shaped everything that followed.
points: Marxism sees history as a class struggle. Capitalism creates an industrial working class (the proletariat) that will overthrow it, which is why Russian Marxists welcomed industrialisation: it was creating the class that would make revolution.
The Russian Social Democratic Labour Party was Marxist and was founded in 1898. At its second congress in 1903 it split into the Bolsheviks under Lenin and the Mensheviks under Martov.

The Socialist Revolutionary Party (SRs), founded in 1901-02, was based on the peasantry, because its members believed Russia's revolution would rest on the land-hungry peasants rather than on factory workers.
The Union of Liberation, founded in 1903-04, was made up of liberals who wanted a constitution, meaning written rules limiting the tsar's power.
notes.tip: Examiners expect you to tell the parties apart: Bolsheviks (Lenin), Mensheviks (Martov), SRs (peasant socialists) and liberals seeking a constitution.

notes.h: Witte's industrialisation: aims and how it was paid for
notes.b: Sergei Witte, Finance Minister from 1892 to 1903, led a state-directed 'great spurt' of industrial growth. Russia had little private capital, so the state had to find the money and direct the effort itself.
points: Witte believed industry was needed for Russia to remain a Great Power, because military strength rested on factories and railways. The state built railways, placed orders with factories and protected industry with tariffs (taxes on imports), including the high tariff of 1891.

Foreign loans and investment paid for mines, ironworks and railways. They came chiefly from France, also from Belgium, Britain and Germany. The Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894 was the channel that made French money flow.
Russia put the rouble on the gold standard in 1897. This meant the rouble could be exchanged for a fixed amount of gold, which reassured foreign investors that their money would keep its value.
Heavy indirect taxes (taxes on goods such as sugar and vodka, paid by everyone) and grain exports provided the rest of the money. Peasants bore most of this burden.
Witte's predecessor, Ivan Vyshnegradsky (Finance Minister 1887-92), had already pushed grain exports. The remark 'We shall go hungry, but we shall export' is usually attributed to him.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Witte with his predecessor Vyshnegradsky (grain exports) or with Stolypin (land reform and repression). Give dated facts: Finance Minister 1892-1903, foreign loans and the gold standard in 1897.

notes.h: Railways, regions and the pace of growth
notes.b: Railways were the heart of the spurt. They tied a vast country together, carried raw materials and goods, and created demand for iron, coal and steel.
points: The Trans-Siberian Railway was begun in 1891. A through route to Vladivostok was open by about 1904, running partly across Manchuria, and the all-Russian route along the Amur was completed in 1916.
The railway network nearly doubled in the 1890s, from about 30,000 km to about 53,000 km, which is why iron and coal industries grew so fast.
Coal and iron grew in the Donbas (the Donets basin) in Ukraine, oil in Baku in the Caucasus, and engineering and textiles in St Petersburg and Moscow.
Industrial output grew at about 8 per cent a year in the 1890s. Coal and pig-iron output (iron fresh from the furnace, the raw material for steel) roughly tripled between 1890 and 1900.
notes.tip: Strong answers on Witte give regions and industries as well as dates: coal and iron in the Donbas, oil at Baku, and engineering and textiles in St Petersburg and Moscow.

notes.h: The costs and limits of the great spurt
notes.b: Rapid growth brought real power but also real strain. The same policies that built factories squeezed the peasants and gathered discontented workers together.
points: Industry was concentrated in huge factories such as the Putilov works in St Petersburg, which had about 12,000 workers in 1905 and tens of thousands during the war. Large crowds of workers made organisation and protest easier.
The peasantry carried the burden through taxes, and grain was exported even in hungry years, so the countryside paid for the towns.
The industrial depression of 1900-03 caused unemployment and strikes. Witte moved out of the Finance Ministry in August 1903.
Growth was rapid again from about 1908 to 1914. By 1914 Russia was often ranked the fifth industrial power in the world by total output, which is an estimate.

Output per head was still low, because the huge peasant population produced little, and dependence on foreign capital was high. Germany's industry, by contrast, grew through private banks and firms rather than the state.
notes.tip: A good Ordinary answer ends with a result: growth set against the burden on the peasants and the discontent of workers. Explain this social result of state-led industrialisation.

notes.h: The peasants and the 1891 famine
notes.b: Most Russians were peasants, and their lives were getting harder. In 1891 a harvest failure turned long-running poverty into a national disaster that damaged the regime's standing.
points: Peasants faced small plots, old methods, rapid population growth and redemption payments. Land hunger (too many people for too little land) grew as families increased.

The harvest failed in 1891 across the Volga and the central black-earth provinces (the rich soil belt), causing famine in 1891-92. Cholera and typhus followed in 1892, and deaths are estimated at about 375,000 to 500,000.

Government relief was slow. Zemstvo and private volunteers, including Leo Tolstoy and Anton Chekhov, organised famine relief, which showed that educated Russians were doing what the state failed to do.
The famine discredited the regime and revived opposition among educated Russians, such as the liberals of the Union of Liberation (1903-04) and the SRs (1901-02).
Peasant unrest grew, with attacks on estates in Kharkov and Poltava provinces in 1902 and far wider violence in 1905-06.
Workers were mostly first-generation peasants who kept links with their villages. This spread discontent between town and country.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why the 1891 famine mattered. The answer is that it discredited the government and revived opposition.

notes.h: The Russo-Japanese War, 1904-05
notes.b: Russia's rivalry with Japan in the Far East led to a war it was confident of winning. Defeat instead exposed the regime's weakness and set off revolution at home.
points: Russia and Japan were rivals over Manchuria and Korea. Russia had leased Port Arthur from China in 1898, and the Trans-Siberian Railway gave it a route east.

Vyacheslav von Plehve, Minister of the Interior from 1902 until he was assassinated in July 1904, is reported to have wanted 'a short victorious war' to distract Russians from discontent. The war had the opposite effect.
Japan attacked the Russian fleet at Port Arthur on the night of 8-9 February 1904, before declaring war. Port Arthur surrendered on 2 January 1905.
Russia lost the land battle of Mukden in February-March 1905. The Baltic Fleet, which had sailed right around the world, was destroyed at Tsushima on 27-28 May 1905.

The Treaty of Portsmouth (New Hampshire, USA) of 5 September 1905 was mediated by President Theodore Roosevelt. Japan gained southern Sakhalin, the Port Arthur lease and recognition of its control of Korea.
Defeat humiliated the autocracy and exposed the weakness of the army, transport and administration, so it was the trigger of the 1905 revolution.
notes.tip: Do not mix up Port Arthur (lost, surrendered January 1905), Mukden (a land battle) and Tsushima (the naval battle). Examiners ask why this war caused revolution.

notes.h: The 1905 Revolution: Bloody Sunday to the October Manifesto
notes.b: Defeat abroad and hardship at home produced a year of revolt. The tsar's response moved from bullets to concessions in a matter of months.
points: On 22 January 1905 (9 January in the Russian calendar) Father Georgy Gapon led a procession to the Winter Palace to petition the tsar. Troops fired on it. The official figure was about 130 dead, though other estimates run to several hundred or more.

Bloody Sunday broke the people's faith in the tsar as their protector, the 'little father'. Strikes, peasant risings, the mutiny on the battleship Potemkin (Black Sea Fleet, June 1905) and national movements in Poland and the Caucasus followed.
In October 1905 a general strike paralysed the railways and cities. The St Petersburg Soviet (council) of Workers' Deputies was formed, with Trotsky as its leading figure.

On Witte's advice the tsar issued the October Manifesto on 30 October 1905 (17 October in the Russian calendar). It promised civil liberties, an elected Duma (parliament) with power over laws, and a wider franchise (more people able to vote).
Witte then became the first chairman of the Council of Ministers, in effect prime minister, serving from October 1905 to April 1906.
notes.tip: For Bloody Sunday, say that figures vary and use 'hundreds killed and wounded'. Remember the Manifesto date is the Russian one, 17 October.

notes.h: Why the tsar survived 1905: the Manifesto and the Fundamental Laws
notes.b: Despite a year of revolt, the regime held on. It split its enemies, kept the army, found money abroad and then took back much of what it had promised.
points: The Manifesto split the opposition. The Octobrists (led by Alexander Guchkov) accepted it. The Constitutional Democrats or Kadets (led by Pavel Milyukov) wanted a constituent assembly and more power for the Duma, and the socialists rejected it.
The army stayed loyal once peace had been made with Japan, so the tsar could use force. The Soviet's leaders were arrested in December 1905 and the Moscow armed rising was crushed that month.
Redemption payments were halved for 1906 and abolished from 1 January 1907, a concession to the peasants announced in November 1905.
A very large French-led international loan in April 1906, about 2,250 million francs, let the government survive without depending on the Duma for money.
The Fundamental Laws of 6 May 1906 (23 April in the Russian calendar) were published shortly before the First Duma met. The tsar remained 'Supreme Autocrat', since the word 'unlimited' was dropped.
He appointed ministers, controlled the army and foreign policy and had an absolute veto over laws. He could dissolve the Duma and issue emergency decrees when it was not sitting (Article 87).
An upper house, the State Council, was half appointed, so it balanced the elected Duma in the tsar's favour.
notes.tip: The comparison examiners reward most is why the tsar survived 1905 but fell in 1917: army loyal and opposition split in 1905, against mutiny and exhaustion in 1917. Keep the Manifesto (promises) separate from the Fundamental Laws (limits).

notes.h: The Dumas and Stolypin's repression
notes.b: Peter Stolypin, Prime Minister from July 1906 to September 1911, combined repression with reform. The Dumas show how little real power the elected parliament had.
points: The First Duma (May-July 1906) demanded land reform and ministers responsible to it. It was dissolved after about 72 days. The Second Duma (February-June 1907) was also dissolved.
In June 1907 the electoral law was changed by decree (the 'coup of 3 June'). Landowners and the wealthy then dominated the Third Duma (1907-12) and the Fourth Duma (1912-17).
The Duma became a place for criticism but not control, because the tsar kept his veto and could still dissolve it.

Stolypin, also Minister of the Interior, crushed disorder with field courts-martial from August 1906. More than a thousand people were executed, and the hangman's noose became known as 'Stolypin's necktie'.
notes.tip: Examiners reward the paired judgement of Stolypin as reformer against Stolypin as repressor. Do not swap him with Witte: Stolypin is land reform and repression, Witte is industrialisation and the Manifesto.

notes.h: Stolypin's land reform and the end of the experiment
notes.b: Stolypin wanted to win the peasants over by making them owners. He needed time, and he did not get it.
points: The land decree of November 1906 let peasants leave the commune, own land privately and consolidate their strips into single farms. The Peasant Land Bank lent them money to buy land.
Resettlement of millions of peasants in Siberia was encouraged. The aim was a loyal class of prosperous peasants, often called a 'wager on the strong', meaning the sober and hardworking peasants.
By 1914 about two million households, roughly a fifth to a quarter depending on how they are counted, had left the commune. Most peasants stayed in it.
Stolypin said that if the state gave him twenty years of peace, Russia would be transformed. This is a paraphrase, not a quotation.
Dmitri Bogrov, a revolutionary who was also a police informer, shot Stolypin at the Kiev opera in September 1911 with Nicholas II present. Stolypin died a few days later.
Protest revived after 1912. Troops shot striking miners at the Lena goldfields in Siberia in April 1912, killing well over a hundred, and large strikes broke out in St Petersburg in July 1914.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why Stolypin failed: too little time, most peasants stayed in the commune, his assassination and the tsar's distrust. Give the household figure as about two million, roughly a fifth to a quarter.

notes.h: The impact of World War I
notes.b: A world war is a war between great alliances that spreads across continents and draws on a country's whole economy and population. Russia's economy and government could not stand that strain, and the war pushed an already weak regime towards collapse.
points: Russia mobilised a huge army, but it was poorly equipped. It lost at Tannenberg in August 1914 and the Masurian Lakes in September 1914, both German victories in East Prussia. The great retreat of 1915 lost Russian Poland.
The Brusilov offensive of June-September 1916 against Austria-Hungary succeeded but at heavy cost. Over the war Russia suffered millions of dead, wounded and prisoners.
About 15 million men were mobilised between 1914 and 1917, which took labour from the farms and cut food output. Railways were overloaded, so food and fuel could not reach the cities.

Inflation rose as the government printed money. The state also lost revenue when the sale of vodka was banned in 1914, because the vodka monopoly had been a major source of income. Food and fuel were short in the cities by winter 1916-17.

Nicholas II took personal command at army headquarters in September 1915. This left Empress Alexandra, who was German-born and so suspected, and Rasputin influential in government, and ministers changed rapidly.
The Progressive Bloc, formed in the Duma in August 1915, demanded a government with public confidence.

Grigori Rasputin was a peasant mystic whom the empress trusted because he seemed to ease the haemophilia of the heir, Alexei. Prince Felix Yusupov and other aristocrats murdered him in December 1916, a sign of the regime's isolation.
notes.tip: On world war, explain how total war broke the Russian economy and state: shortages, overloaded railways and inflation as well as defeats. Name the battles only for their effect on Russia.

notes.h: The February Revolution, 1917
notes.b: The regime that had survived 1905 fell in a few days in 1917. The key difference was that this time the soldiers refused to fire on the crowds.
points: On 8 March 1917 (23 February in the Russian calendar), International Women's Day, women textile workers in Petrograd demanded bread. Their strikes grew into a general strike in the city.
The garrison regiments mutinied on 12 March (27 February) and joined the crowds instead of firing on them. This was the key difference from 1905, when the army stayed loyal.
On the same day the Duma set up a Provisional Committee and the Petrograd Soviet of Workers' and Soldiers' Deputies was revived.
The generals advised abdication. Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March (2 March) at Pskov, for himself and Alexei, and his brother Grand Duke Michael declined the throne the next day.
This ended about 300 years of Romanov rule, which had begun in 1613.
notes.tip: Say about 300 years of Romanov rule, not exactly 300. The garrison joining the crowds is the key difference from 1905, so state it clearly.

notes.h: The Provisional Government and dual power
notes.b: After the tsar fell, two bodies claimed authority. The new government's decisions on war and land gave the Bolsheviks their chance.
points: Prince Georgy Lvov headed the Provisional Government from March to July 1917, and Alexander Kerensky from July. It shared authority with the Petrograd Soviet, an arrangement called 'dual power' (dvoevlastie).
The Soviet's Order No. 1, issued in March 1917, told soldiers to obey the Provisional Government's military orders only if the Soviet agreed. This weakened the government's control of the army.

The government granted civil liberties but kept fighting the war and postponed land reform until a Constituent Assembly could meet. The failed July (Kerensky) offensive of 1917 brought more desertions, and peasants began to seize land.
Lenin returned to Petrograd's Finland Station in April 1917 (16 April; 3 April in the Russian calendar), crossing Germany by train with German permission. He issued the April Theses.
The Theses demanded 'All power to the Soviets' and promised 'Peace, land and bread'. These slogans appealed to soldiers, peasants and hungry workers.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why the Provisional Government fell: it continued the war and delayed land reform. Do not confuse the Soviet (council), the Duma (parliament) and the Provisional Government (ministers drawn from the Duma).

notes.h: The Bolshevik seizure of power, October 1917
notes.b: Within months of the April Theses the Bolsheviks went from a small party to the rulers of Petrograd. Failure by their opponents and careful organisation by Trotsky made this possible.
points: The July Days of July 1917 were a failed Bolshevik-backed rising, and Lenin went into hiding in Finland.

General Lavr Kornilov, commander-in-chief, moved troops towards Petrograd in mid-September 1917 (late August / early September in the Russian calendar). Kerensky armed the Petrograd workers (Red Guards) and released Bolshevik prisoners. The Kornilov affair thus armed the Red Guards and boosted the Bolsheviks.

The Bolsheviks won majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets in September. Trotsky became chairman of the Petrograd Soviet from October (late September) and organised its Military Revolutionary Committee.

The rising began on 6-7 November (24-25 October in the Russian calendar). Bolshevik forces seized the stations, bridges and telegraph, and the Winter Palace was taken in the early hours of 8 November (26 October).
The Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets met on 7-8 November (25-26 October). It approved the Council of People's Commissars (Sovnarkom), with Lenin as chairman.

The Decree on Peace and the Decree on Land followed on 8 November (26 October), together with the Declaration of the Rights of the Peoples of Russia. The Cheka (the Bolshevik secret police) was founded in December 1917 under Felix Dzerzhinsky.

In the Constituent Assembly election of November 1917 the SRs won about 40 per cent of the vote and the Bolsheviks about 24 per cent, about a quarter. The Assembly met once, on 18-19 January 1918 (5-6 January), and was dispersed by Red Guards.
notes.tip: Do not say the Winter Palace fell on the night of 6-7 November: it was taken in the early hours of 8 November. Keep the Kornilov (general) and Kolchak (admiral, White leader) apart, and the Cheka apart from the tsarist Okhrana.

notes.h: Brest-Litovsk and the end of the war with Germany
notes.b: The Bolsheviks had promised peace, but Germany demanded a high price. The treaty shows how weak the new government was.
points: An armistice (a halt in fighting) with Germany was agreed in December 1917. Trotsky, Commissar for Foreign Affairs, stalled at Brest-Litovsk with a policy of 'neither war nor peace', hoping revolution would spread.
Germany advanced again in February 1918, so the Bolsheviks gave in. A Soviet delegation signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918.

Russia lost Poland, the Baltic provinces (Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia), Finland and Ukraine. This was about a third of the population of European Russia, with much of its coal, industry and farmland.
The treaty was cancelled after Germany's defeat in November 1918.
The capital moved from Petrograd to Moscow in March 1918, away from the German threat.
notes.tip: Examiners expect two wars and two revolutions in order, running on to Brest-Litovsk and the civil war when the question reaches 1920. Do not stop at 1917, and give no exact percentages for the losses.

notes.h: The civil war, 1918-20
notes.b: Within months the Bolsheviks faced armed enemies at home and abroad. They won, and the reasons why are a favourite exam question.
points: The Romanovs, Nicholas II, Alexandra and their children, were shot at Ekaterinburg on 16-17 July 1918, so no tsar could become a rallying point for the Whites.

The civil war was fought between the Reds (the Bolsheviks) and the Whites, a loose mix of generals, monarchists and liberals: Admiral Kolchak in Siberia, General Denikin in the south, General Yudenich in the north-west against Petrograd and General Wrangel in the Crimea in 1920.

Trotsky, Commissar for War from March 1918, built the Red Army and used tens of thousands of former tsarist officers, watched by political commissars. The Czech Legion, former prisoners of war, revolted along the Trans-Siberian Railway in May 1918.
Britain (at Murmansk and Archangel), Japan and the USA (at Vladivostok) and France in the south landed troops from 1918. Their effect was limited.
War Communism (1918-21) meant seizing grain from peasants, nationalising industry and rationing. The Red Terror was launched in September 1918 after an attempt on Lenin's life in August 1918.

Kolchak was defeated in 1919 and executed in February 1920. Yudenich was turned back near Petrograd in October 1919. Denikin's advance on Moscow was defeated in autumn 1919 and he resigned in 1920. Wrangel was evacuated from the Crimea in November 1920.
The Reds held the central core with its railways, industry, the capitals and the largest population, so they could move troops. They had one command and one aim.

The Whites were divided and scattered, and were linked to landlords and foreign powers, so many peasants feared their return. In the Polish-Soviet war of 1919-20 the Red Army's advance on Warsaw was defeated in August 1920.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why the Reds won the civil war, so give several causes with reasons. Confine War Communism to 1918-21 and leave out the later New Economic Policy.

notes.h: Key concept: self-determination
notes.b: Self-determination was one of the most powerful ideas of the period, and the revolution gave it a particular Russian shape. Examiners ask how it was applied and how it was denied.
points: Self-determination is the right of a people to choose its own government and state.

The Bolsheviks applied it in the Declaration of the Rights of the Peoples of Russia in November 1917, which recognised the right of peoples to self-determination. Finland declared independence in December 1917 and the Soviet government recognised it at the end of December 1917 or January 1918.
Poland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania became independent in 1918, confirmed by treaties with Soviet Russia in 1920. Poland's border was settled in 1921.
It was denied elsewhere: the Red Army brought Ukraine and other borderlands back under Bolshevik rule. For Lenin, self-determination came second to the revolution.
notes.tip: On self-determination, set the Bolshevik declaration and the new states against the Red Army's reconquest of the borderlands.

notes.h: Assessment: modernisation, crisis and revolution
notes.b: Tsarist Russia was changing fast, but its political system could not keep up. Judgement questions reward answers that weigh achievements against limits and long-term against short-term causes.
points: Achievement: Witte built railways and heavy industry, growth resumed after 1908, and Stolypin began to create a class of independent farmers.
Limit: growth rested on foreign capital and a poor peasantry, and it created a discontented working class in huge factories.

Limit: political reform stopped short, because the Dumas were weak. Nicholas II mistrusted reformers, with Witte let go in 1906 and Stolypin's position weak by 1911, and he wasted the chance of 1905-06.

Why the regime survived 1905 but fell in 1917: in 1905 the army stayed loyal and the opposition was split. In 1917 the army was exhausted, the cities were starving and the soldiers joined the strikers.
Long-term causes (economic backwardness, autocracy, the peasantry) set against the short-term cause (the war) is the central judgement. Decide which mattered most and show how one led to the other.

Historians: the 'optimists' argue Russia was modernising and the war caused the collapse. The 'pessimists' argue revolution was likely anyway. Leopold Haimson pointed to the 1912-14 strike wave, and Orlando Figes stresses the regime's failure to reform.

Alexander Gerschenkron argued that in a backward country the state substitutes for missing private capital, with Witte as the example. Richard Pipes sees October as a coup by a minority party, while Soviet historians saw a popular workers' revolution.
Contemporary views: liberals blamed the tsar's obstinacy, and the Bolsheviks presented October as a workers' revolution. Opponents called it a seizure of power by a minority party.
notes.tip: For the commonest Higher essay on crisis or collapse, open with a clear judgement that weighs long-term causes against the war, then show how each led to the next. Also weigh Witte's achievement against its cost, and October 1917 as a popular revolution against a coup, naming a historian.

keyTerms.definition: A war fought across several continents by many states and empires, which in Russia's case led to military defeat, economic breakdown and revolution.
The principle that peoples may choose their own government and state; the Bolsheviks proclaimed it in November 1917, and Finland, Poland and the Baltic states became independent.
Rule by a monarch with unlimited power, as claimed by the tsars and preserved in the Fundamental Laws of 1906.
The Russian peasant commune, which held land collectively and redistributed strips among its households.
The Russian elected parliament created in 1905-06 with limited powers; four Dumas met before 1917.
The decree of 17 October 1905 promising civil liberties and an elected Duma, issued on Witte's advice to end the revolution.
A council of workers' and soldiers' deputies, first formed in St Petersburg in 1905 and revived in 1917.
The shared authority in 1917 between the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet.
The faction of the Russian Social Democrats led by Lenin, who seized power in November 1917.
The Bolshevik economic policy during the civil war of requisitioning grain, nationalising industry and rationing.

factCards.term: Emancipation of the serfs: date and terms
factCards.definition: 1861 under Alexander II; peasants paid redemption payments over 49 years for their land.
Railway building (Trans-Siberian), the gold standard in 1897, and foreign loans, mainly from France.
Harvest failure hit the Volga and black earth provinces; the slow government response weakened trust in the regime.
Japan attacked Port Arthur on 8 February 1904; Russia lost Mukden and the Baltic Fleet was destroyed at Tsushima (May 1905); Portsmouth treaty, September 1905.
Troops fired on a peaceful procession led by Father Gapon to the Winter Palace, killing and wounding hundreds.
Issued 17 October 1905: civil liberties, a wider franchise and an elected Duma with legislative powers.
Kept the Tsar's autocratic powers: control of ministers, army and foreign policy, the veto, and rule by decree.
Land reform of 1906 let peasants leave the commune and own land; field courts-martial hanged revolutionaries.

factCards.term: When did the February Revolution begin?
factCards.definition: On 8 March 1917 (23 February in the old calendar), when Petrograd women's demonstrations grew into a general strike and mutiny.
On 15 March 1917, ending Romanov rule after about 300 years.
Issued after his return in April 1917, demanding all power to the Soviets, peace, land and bread.

factCards.term: When did the Bolsheviks seize power?
factCards.definition: On 6-7 November 1917 (24-25 October in the old calendar), with the capture of the Winter Palace.

factCards.term: Treaty of Brest-Litovsk: date and losses
factCards.definition: 3 March 1918; Russia gave up Poland, the Baltic provinces, Ukraine and Finland.

factCards.term: Why did the Reds win the civil war?
factCards.definition: They held the central territory with railways and industry, had a united command under Trotsky, and the Whites were divided and feared by peasants.

factCards.term: Why did the regime survive 1905 but fall in 1917?
factCards.definition: In 1905 the army stayed loyal and the opposition split after the October Manifesto; in 1917 the exhausted army joined the strikers.
